paragraphs.text: A tuo of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from 1980. The style’s warm, damp pile was devised to give in weeks the cup that Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er kept for years. Yunnan’s state factories brought [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973, and by 1975 the [method worked out at Menghai](shou:piling-1973) had settled into the ripe pu’er still made today. This tea was made seven years after that start, in the style’s first decade.
Its leaf grew in Menghai County. The county is not the same as [Menghai Tea Factory](menghai-county:county-and-factory), and nothing in this tea’s record ties it to the factory.

At forty-six years old, it has long since become what the trade calls [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf is still changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so how it has been stored shapes it as much as its age does.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.

unsupported.why: The origin field says only "Menghai, Yunnan, China". The county-and-factory claim says Menghai on a label can mean the county or the factory, and that the factory's ripe tea sometimes uses leaf from outside the county, such as Lincang. So nothing supports saying the leaf itself grew in the county.
